newsitem.title: INDIA: India's RBI intervenes to halt rupee surge vs dlr.
newsitem.headline: India's RBI intervenes to halt rupee surge vs dlr.

text.p: The Indian rupee softened on Friday after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) intervened to cap the currency's gains but it remained around its strongest level for seven months against the U.S. dollar, dealers said.
In mid-afternoon trade, the rupee was quoted at 35.705/712 per dollar after touching 35.69 earlier.
Dealers said the RBI bought dollars and weakened the rupee after the unit broke a key level.

"I think the RBI decided to step in once the rupee breached 35.70," said the chief dealer at a European bank. "The rupee was on a one-way trip upwards till the RBI came in. But they bought in small amounts...looks like they only wanted to make an appearance."
On Thursday the rupee touched its strongest level in seven months of 35.735 against the dollar, after opening at 35.755/765, on poor dollar demand and central bank inaction.
The RBI's absence from the foreign exchange market on Thursday triggered speculation on whether the central bank would check the rupee's gains or let market forces determine the exchange rate.
The Business Standard daily said on Friday that the RBI had decided not to intervene unless there was an "extreme provocation".
The decision was made after a meeting between RBI governor Chakravarty Rangarajan and finance minister P. Chidambaram last Saturday, the newspaper said.
An RBI spokesperson declined to comment on the report.
The spokesperson said the RBI's intervention policy was guided by the demand-supply situation in the market and it sought to even out any mismatches.
The other objective was to keep the value of the rupee close to the real effective exchange rate, the spokesperson added.
Indian exporters have in recent months been complaining about the exchange rate, saying the rupee was overvalued and its strength would affect their competitiveness in international markets.
On Friday, neighbouring Pakistan devalued its currency.
Dealers said the move was a technical correction to adjust for the U.S. dollar's appreciation against major currencies worldwide.
Indian exports grew only four percent to $33.1 billion in 1996/97 (April-March) compared to 21.4 percent growth the previous year.

"Part of the reason for the rupee's rise since yesterday is that some banks were holding long dollar positions," said a dealer. "The general market expectation was that RBI would buy dollars at 35.75 and check the rupee's rise but this didn't happen."
"Banks were forced to unwind their longs on Thursday when the RBI didn't come in as the rupee hit 35.75," he said.
"There was no sign of the RBI today till (the) afternoon and this again led to selling. In recent times the only demand has been from RBI," he said.
"When they are away, even normal supplies do not get absorbed by the market and push the rupee up."

The rupee has been buoyant for the past year due to healthy inflows of dollars supply and poor demand for the U.S. unit. Inflows have been mainly from foreign investment and foreign currency borrowings by Indian corporates.
India's foreign currency reserves leapt to $25.4 billion on June 27 from $19.7 billion on February 28.
